senses.definition: (anatomy) The part of the body connecting the head and the trunk found in humans and some animals.

quotes.text: Mother, help me, there's a head attached to my neck and I'm in it.
quotes.reference: 2019 October 15, ZA/UM, Robert Kurvitz, quoting You, Disco Elysium, →OCLC:

senses.definition: The corresponding part in some other anatomical contexts.
The part of a shirt, dress etc., which fits a person's neck.
The tapered part of a bottle toward the opening.
(botany) The slender tubelike extension atop an archegonium, through which the sperm swim to reach the egg.

quotes.text: Archegonia are surrounded early in their development by the juvenile perianth, through the slender beak of which the elongated neck of the fertilized archegonium protrudes.
quotes.reference: 1992, Rudolf M[athias] Schuster, The Hepaticae and Anthocerotae of North America: East of the Hundredth Meridian, volume V, Chicago, Ill.: Field Museum of Natural History, →ISBN, page 5:

senses.definition: (music) The extension of any stringed instrument on which a fingerboard is mounted
A long narrow tract of land projecting from the main body, or a narrow tract connecting two larger tracts.
(engineering) A reduction in size near the end of an object, formed by a groove around it.
examples: a neck forming the journal of a shaft

senses.definition: The constriction between the root and crown of a tooth.
(architecture) The gorgerin of a capital.
(geology) A volcanic plug, solidified lava filling the vent of an extinct volcano.
(firearms) The small part of a gun between the chase and the swell of the muzzle.
(figurative) A person's life.
examples: to risk one's neck; to save someone's neck

senses.definition: (informal, MLE, slang) A falsehood; a lie.
(slang) Fellatio

quotes.text:
Shorty throw neck like a geese
She make me speak Portuguese
She drop neck for a check and a paystub
quotes.reference: 2018, “Florida Thang”, in The South Got Something To Say, performed by Pouya:

senses.definition: (now historical) A bundle of wheat used in certain English harvest ceremonies.

quotes.text: The person with 'the neck' stands in the centre, grasping it with both his hands
quotes.reference: 1837, R. A. R., The Everyday Book, page 1169:

quotes.text: "The neck" is generally hung up in the farmhouse, where it remains for two or three years.
quotes.reference: 1911, James George Frazer, The Golden Bough, volume 7, page 266:

senses.definition: (transitive, slang) To hang by the neck; strangle; kill, eliminate.
(intransitive, informal, chiefly US) To intently kiss or cuddle; to canoodle.
examples: Alan and Betty were necking in the back of a car when Betty's dad caught them.

quotes.text: Molly had been in love with Sick Boy since he necked with her in a seedy disco-bar in Leith a few weeks ago. Sick Boy had made a drunken point about HIV transmission and to illustrate it had spent most of the night french-kissing her.
quotes.reference: 1994 [1993], Irvine Welsh, Trainspotting, London: Minerva, →ISBN, page 326:

senses.definition: (transitive, slang) To drink or swallow rapidly.

quotes.text: Actually, mostly I swan around in my silver sports car, necking drugs, and feeling sorry for myself.
In the dim light, punters sit sipping raspberry-flavoured Tokyo martinis, losing the freestyle sushi off their chopsticks or necking Asahi beer.
The 40-year-old [Mike Skinner] is happy to put his body on the line in other ways, swapping a mug of tea for a fan's double pint of lager and messily necking it in one.

senses.definition: (intransitive) To decrease in diameter.

quotes.text: Since this temperature would place the bolt in its creep range, it will slowly stretch, necking down as it does so. Eventually it will get too thin to support the weight, and the bolt will break.

senses.definition: (folklore) A shapeshifting water spirit in Germanic mythology and folklore; a nix.

quotes.text:
The Neck no more upon the river sings.
And no Mermaid to bleach her linen flings
Upon the waves in the mild solar ray.
quotes.reference: 1828, Thomas Keightley, The Fairy Mythology, volume I, London: William Harrison Ainsworth, page 234:

quotes.text: The beautiful Nix or Nixie who allures the young fisher or hunter to seek her embraces in the wave which brings his death, the Neck who seizes upon and drowns the maidens who sport upon his banks, the river-spirit who still yearly in some parts of Germany demands tribute of human life, are all forms of the ancient Nicor[.]
